title: Block: Multi-Source BFS on a Grid
oneLiner: For every cell in a 0/1 grid, return the distance to the nearest 0, by starting BFS from all the zeros at once.
keyTakeaway: Multi-source BFS puts every source in the queue before the loop starts. One BFS from all of them is the same as many BFS runs taking the minimum, in a fraction of the time.
explanation:
grid holds 0s and 1s and has at least one 0. Return a grid of the same shape where each cell is the number of up, down, left or right steps to the nearest 0.

Fill a distance grid with -1, then enqueue every 0 cell with distance 0. Pop cells in order; for each of the four neighbours inside the grid that is still -1, set it to the popped cell's distance plus one and enqueue it. Rotting Oranges and Walls and Gates are this block.

starterCode.python:
def distance_to_zero(grid):
    # 1. Make a distance grid the same shape, filled with -1.
    # 2. Put every 0 cell in the queue with distance 0: all the sources start together.
    # 3. Take cells from the front of the queue in order.
    # 4. For each neighbour inside the grid still at -1, set it to the cell's distance plus 1 and enqueue it.
    # 5. Return the distance grid.
    return grid

gotchas: Running a separate BFS from each 1 (or each 0), which is O((n · m)²).
Enqueuing a neighbour without marking it, so it is reached again at a larger distance.

complexity.note: Each of the n · m cells is enqueued once and checks four neighbours; the distance grid and queue are n · m.
